draft.title: The Victorian court hierarchy
card: Victorian courts are ranked in a hierarchy. From the bottom up, the main courts are the Magistrates' Court, the County Court and the Supreme Court.
the power of a court to hear a case for the first time. Each court can hear only the types of case its jurisdiction allows.
the power of a court to hear an appeal, which asks a higher court to review a decision made by a lower court.

Less serious matters usually begin in the Magistrates' Court, and more serious ones in the County Court or Supreme Court. So each case goes to a court suited to it, and a party who thinks a decision was wrong can ask a higher court to review it.
draft.remember: The hierarchy matches cases to suitable courts and lets decisions be appealed upward.

a.q: Why does Victoria have a court hierarchy, with different courts hearing different cases?
opts: Cases go to courts suited to them, and appeals are possible
Every case is heard by each court in turn, from the bottom
Lower courts only hear cases that parliament has just changed
Higher courts decide every case so that no appeals are needed
a.why: A ranking lets serious or complex cases go to higher courts, and lets a party ask a higher court to review a decision. The option about every court hearing each case is wrong because cases usually begin in one court, not all of them.
a.clue: Think about matching a case to a court and about reviewing a decision.

b.q: Sam is unhappy with a decision made in the Magistrates' Court and asks the County Court to review it. Which power is the County Court using?
opts: Appellate jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction
Statutory interpretation
Precedent
b.why: The County Court is reviewing a decision from a lower court, which is appellate jurisdiction. Original jurisdiction is wrong because that is hearing a case for the first time, and Sam's case has already been decided.
b.clue: Has this case already been decided once?
